newsitem.title: USA: Venezuela to use oil windfall for debt fund -Matos.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela to use oil windfall for debt fund -Matos.

text.p: Venezuela plans to use most of its windfall oil revenues for a special debt repayment fund, the country's finance minister said here on Friday.

Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar told Reuters Financial Television that the government's three main economic goals were to maintain fiscal discipline, pursue restructuring including privatization, and channel the excess oil income toward debt payment.
"We are going to create a fund to guarantee that we can fulfill the schedule of payments and we will not have the story that we had in the past in Venezuela," Matos said.

He estimated the government would reap about $800 million in extra oil revenue by the end of 1996. The extra revenue has come from petroleum prices that have risen well above the country's budget projections.

"That (money) we plan to sterilize ... use it for a fund that we are working on together with Congress to guarantee the payment of the debt and use mechanisms to reduce debt service over the long term," he said.
He said the oil revenue fund would mainly be applied to internal debt, but also be used for external debt.

Venezuela would pay its interest arrears on domestic debt with last week's placement of 650 million mark-denominated paper, and the country plans to be up-to-date with the Paris Club for 1996, Matos said.
Venezuela does not have any immediate plans to return to the international markets for financing, but wants to keep its options open for the future, Matos said.
The minister also said that "a small amount" of the oil fund would also be directed to a special dollar-denominated account as the first step in creating a private pension fund system.

He said that a team from the International Monetary Fund evaluating the Venezuelan economy was pleased with the progress of economic variables, particularly data showing GDP fell only 3.5 percent in the first half of 1996, rather than a projected 5.0 percent drop.
"The upturn has begun already," he said. "Exports are growing again after declining the last five months and consumption has begun to increase, and inflation has been under control."
The government aims to bring inflation down to 25 percent inflation along with 4.0 percent growth in 1997, he said.
Venezuela would likely commence discussions with the IMF in about two to three months for an extended fund facility.
Regarding the banking sector, Matos said the government would probably decrease the size of a planned capitalization fund and employ other mechanisms to stimulate the sector.
